assessmentSummary.identity: A high-impact composite that is provisionally interpreted as a bilateral half-turn jump, a bilateral landing, an immediate second rebound, and a short acceleration. The legacy card does not establish whether rebound means a second flight or merely a quick transition from the first landing into the sprint, so the exact contact sequence remains quarantined.
currentCardFindings: The title and description do not identify the takeoff, first landing, second takeoff, second landing, sprint direction, turn side, or whether the rebound is a distinct flight.
The existing three videos demonstrate pro-agility or general deceleration rather than this aerial-turn sequence and must be superseded as direct candidates.
The legacy two-second rest value is incompatible with low-volume high-output work and would convert a precision plyometric sequence into conditioning.
The legacy difficulty scores understate impact, failure consequence, coordination, supervision, and body-mass loading across the landing-to-reacceleration transition.

coachCues: Know the turn and exit before takeoff
athleteInstructions: Jump and turn one half rotation
Land on both feet in the marked area
Complete the assigned rebound without an extra shuffle
Land and accelerate through the exit cone

calibrationEvidence.basis: plyometric reviews, sprint-transfer evidence, current-card comparison, and direct component-video discovery
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: No authoritative source or exact video located in this pass establishes what the legacy author meant by rebound. Difficulty and dose are conservative proposals for the more demanding two-flight interpretation.

assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Keep the card quarantined until rebound is defined. If a second flight is intended, retain one composite card with the exact five-stage contact sequence. If no second flight is intended, rename it 180 Jump to Sprint-Out and model the immediate acceleration as the baseline; do not use pro-agility media as an exact demonstration.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Perform 180 Jump Rebound to Sprint-Out as a low-volume, high-quality plyometric or reactive-output exposure. The exercise targets half-turn rebound linked to a short acceleration. The coach should cap volume, demand clean landings, and stop the set before contact quality fades.

evidence.sourceTitle: Plyometric Training Practices of Brazilian Olympic Sprint and Jump Coaches: Toward a Deeper Understanding of Their Choices and Insights
claims: Plyometric exercise selection varies by movement direction, contact type, intensity, and intended transfer, so the exact sequence is part of exercise identity.
The current name does not establish whether rebound is a second flight. 180 Jump Rebound to Sprint-Out must remain quarantined until takeoff, landing, rebound, and sprint contacts are explicit.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Vertically and Horizontally Orientated Plyometric Training on Physical Performance: A Meta-analytical Comparison
claims: Vertically and horizontally oriented plyometric tasks are not interchangeable and show direction-specific training effects.

Classify 180 Jump Rebound to Sprint-Out by rotational angle, horizontal and vertical projection, takeoff and landing laterality, number of flights, contact sequence, exit direction, and sprint distance.

evidence.sourceTitle: Muscle activity in sprinting: a review
claims: Sprinting uses phase-dependent lower-limb muscle activity across force production, limb recovery, and ground contact.
The card must represent ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, trunk, and arm actions across both landing contacts and the acceleration exit rather than assigning the task to one muscle.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Plyometric Jump Training on the Reactive Strength Index in Healthy Individuals Across the Lifespan: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
claims: Reactive-strength tasks depend on rapid coupling of eccentric landing and concentric takeoff actions.
A pause, extra step, collapsed landing, or undefined second contact changes the proposed reactive sequence and must be logged as a failed or different repetition.
Plyometric demand rises with movement intensity, complexity, and landing requirements and should be progressed from controlled foundations.

Assess technical complexity and physical load directly, with separate coordination, supervision, failure-consequence, impact, work-capacity, and overall scores; do not assign an athlete level to the card.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Plyometric Training on Lower Body Muscle Architecture, Tendon Structure, Stiffness and Physical Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
claims: Plyometric training loads the muscle-tendon unit and produces adaptations that depend on exposure characteristics.
Track high-impact contacts, turn direction, sprint accelerations, landing noise, contact speed, and overlapping jump or sprint work; the legacy two-second rest is not a quality-output prescription.
Safe plyometric progression requires appropriate foundations, surface, space, and exercise selection.

180 Jump Rebound to Sprint-Out requires a high-traction landing area, a clear sprint lane, defined markers, adequate lighting, and demonstrated control of its component jump, rebound, and sprint tasks.

evidence.sourceTitle: Plyometric Training Practices of Brazilian Olympic Sprint and Jump Coaches: Toward a Deeper Understanding of Their Choices and Insights
claims: High-level coaching practice organizes plyometrics by contacts, intensity, exercise type, and recovery rather than treating all jumps as one volume.
The proposed one-to-three-repetition sets and full recovery are conservative programming inferences for quality; they are not a research-validated universal dose for this exact composite.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Vertically and Horizontally Orientated Plyometric Training on Physical Performance: A Meta-analytical Comparison
claims: Projection direction is a meaningful property of plyometric work.
Instructions must name turn direction, takeoff and landing feet, whether a second flight occurs, landing zone, exit direction, sprint distance, reset rule, and what counts as one repetition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Training should use qualified supervision, safe environments, technically appropriate tasks, and gradual progression.
Stop for pain, guarding, dizziness, uncontrolled rotation, extra contacts, repeated collapse, loud landings, slipping, unsafe spacing, or material loss of speed.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effect of Vertical Jump and Sprint Training on Power and Speed Performance Transfer
claims: Jump and sprint training transfer is direction- and task-dependent rather than automatic.
Use 180 Jump Rebound to Sprint-Out only when an athlete needs the defined rotational-contact-to-acceleration transition; do not claim general speed transfer or use it as conditioning.
Progressive plyometric instruction benefits from simple tasks and controlled landings before complex contacts.
Athlete support needs a contact-sequence animation, turn and exit arrows, a successful and failed landing example, repetition count, and a prominent stop cue.

evidence.sourceTitle: Plyometric Training Practices of Brazilian Olympic Sprint and Jump Coaches: Toward a Deeper Understanding of Their Choices and Insights
claims: Coaches manage plyometric exercise type, contact volume, intensity, and placement within training.
Coach support must include layout, side and rear observation, contact counting, turn-side balance, readiness prerequisites, fatigue evidence, and regression decisions.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Exercise selection and progression should match demonstrated movement control and be supervised appropriately.
Accessibility begins by separating the sequence into jump-to-stick, low rebound, and acceleration components, reducing speed and contacts, using visual floor arrows, and permitting extra reset time.

evidence.sourceTitle: Effects of Vertically and Horizontally Orientated Plyometric Training on Physical Performance: A Meta-analytical Comparison
claims: Changing projection direction changes the plyometric task and potential transfer.
A second flight, turn angle, takeoff or landing laterality, reactive cue, run-in, and sprint exit can change identity or variant classification; a 505 shuttle is not the same aerial sequence.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.

The selected links demonstrate only components or adjacent variants. None is represented as an exact full-sequence match, and link health, captions, safety, cue quality, reviewer identity, and approval remain pending.

alternateAssessments.name: 180 Jump to Sprint-Out
alternateAssessments.rationale: If there is no distinct second flight, the primary contact sequence changes from jump-rebound-sprint to jump-land-sprint and should be named directly rather than hidden under rebound.

alternateAssessments.name: 180 Jump to Stick
alternateAssessments.rationale: The deliberate held landing terminates the task and removes the reactive rebound and sprint transition.

alternateAssessments.name: Reactive-Cue 180 Jump Rebound to Sprint-Out
alternateAssessments.rationale: An unpredictable cue adds perception and choice while preserving the same physical sequence; it is a controlled reactive variant only after the baseline identity is resolved.

alternateAssessments.name: Single-Leg 180 Jump Rebound to Sprint-Out
alternateAssessments.rationale: Unilateral takeoff or landing materially changes joint loading, balance demand, laterality, failure consequence, and prerequisites.

alternateAssessments.name: 5-0-5 Change of Direction
alternateAssessments.rationale: A sprint-in 180-degree planted turn has no aerial half-turn or rebound and is a separate change-of-direction identity.
